extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy/natural philosophy (metaphysics, teleology)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of criteria for employing teleological (final-cause) versus mechanistic (efficient-cause) explanations in organized and unorganized nature, and the metaphysical requirement (a will) for teleology to be philosophically coherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleology as a safe guide in organised nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Teleology, as the assumption of the adaptation of every part to its end, is a perfectly safe guide in considering the whole of organised nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use final causes (adaptation/ends) as primary explanatory principle for the origin and arrangement of organs and parts in organisms; when considering anatomy and the form of organisms, seek ends and functions first. Examples: organs whose use is unknown should be assumed to serve the will/maintenance of the organism rather than be dismissed as caprice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficient causes as clue to unorganised nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Efficient causes are the clue to the understanding of unorganised nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For non-organic phenomena (physics, geology, chemistry), explanations should focus on efficient causes (forces, mechanisms). Final-cause explanations are ambiguous or less valid here, and one must usually seek efficient mechanisms to explain unorganised regularities (e.g., reasons for sea salinity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Final causes secondary for metaphysical explanation beyond experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Final causes cannot without violence enter into the connection of any philosophical system except that one which makes a will the basis; they must only be regarded as valid in a secondary and subsidiary manner for metaphysical explanations beyond experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat teleological arguments as confirmatory or secondary when used in metaphysical arguments; teleology can support but not independently establish metaphysical principles unless the system posits will as the basis of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not presume aimlessness of apparently useless parts
rubrics_metrics.description: If in some animal a part is found of which we do not see any use, we must never venture the conjecture that nature has produced it aimlessly, perhaps trifling, or out of mere caprice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain the investigatory assumption that every part in organised nature serves some end related to the organism's will/maintenance; continue searching for possible functions (e.g., historical searches for spleen function) rather than concluding mere chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptio firmat regulam — explain exceptions by inner connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual real exceptions to the universal law of design in organised nature have been discovered, but they can be accounted for upon other grounds (exceptio firmat regulam).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for anomalous organs or rudiments (e.g., male breasts, rudimentary eyes beneath skin) by appeals to unity of type, developmental or phylogenetic connections, or shared structural plans across taxa rather than abandoning teleological interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homology (unité de plan) supplies material for teleology
rubrics_metrics.description: Homology, the fundamental type or 'unité de plan' of animal organization, is the material upon which teleology builds; anatomical elements (homologies) indicate a shared plan that grounds adaptive explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use homologies (e.g., seven cervical vertebrae, analogues of human hand in whale fin) to ground teleological explanations and to explain why certain organs or rudiments persist across related species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear distinction: efficient cause vs final cause
rubrics_metrics.description: The efficient cause is that whereby something is, the final cause that on account of which it is; the phenomenon has, in time, the former behind it and the latter before it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing an event or structure, identify both what brings it about (efficient cause) and what it serves or tends toward (final cause). Recognize that in voluntary animal action these two unite (the motive as final cause appears as the efficient cause).

rubrics_metrics.name: Final cause appears as motive and can act prior to apprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: The final cause is a motive which acts upon a being, by which it is not known; final causes acted before they were apprehended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow that adaptive features may originate because of 'motives' (functional demands) that pre-exist their apprehension by intelligence. Examples: termite nests as motive for ant-bear adaptations; laws of optics as motives for eye structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: In organised nature, efficient causes are subordinate/tools
rubrics_metrics.description: In organised nature, efficient causes assume only a quite subordinate position as the mere tools of the final causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat mechanistic/efficiency accounts as instruments that realize ends; for origin of parts and organ form, final causes (ends) provide the main explanatory insight; efficient mechanisms may be unknown or of secondary interest for teleological explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final causes more informative than efficient causes for physiological understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: In explaining physiological functions we look for the efficient causes, though for the most part in vain; but the final cause is far more important and more to the point than the efficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When investigating physiological processes, prioritize understanding the function or 'purpose' (why the process occurs) because knowing the final cause often yields more explanatory power even when the mechanical details are not fully known (example: circulation—knowing purpose of oxygenation clarifies significance even without full efficient-cause account).

rubrics_metrics.name: Both efficient and final causes ideally sought though often only one attainable
rubrics_metrics.description: We are only perfectly content when we know both the efficient cause and the final cause at once and yet separately, but such twofold knowledge is seldom attainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to identify both causes for a full explanation; recognize practical limits (often only final or only efficient cause known) and accept provisional explanations based on whichever is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final causes can give sufficient, perfect explanations within their domain
rubrics_metrics.description: The final cause within its sphere affords a sufficient and perfect explanation; the efficient cause always ultimately rests upon something that cannot be fathomed (a qualitas occulta) and therefore gives only a relative explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on teleological accounts when appropriate because they can fully account for adaptive features, whereas mechanistic accounts may remain relative or incomplete due to hidden forces; but be aware of domain limits of each mode of explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity of external design in physico-theological use
rubrics_metrics.description: External design always remains ambiguous for physico-theological demonstrations and can be misused; there are ateleological instances in contrarium that undermine simplistic appeals to design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise caution when using observed 'design' in nature as evidence of a designer—counterexamples (e.g., sea water being undrinkable despite abundance) show limits of such arguments; avoid overreliance on remote or ambiguous signs of purpose in unorganised contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design may arise from blind forces under natural laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the guidance of cosmogonies like Laplace's, perfectly blind forces of nature acting according to unalterable laws could produce the framework of the world equal to the work of a high combinatorial power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider non-teleological accounts where complex order emerges from blind law-driven processes; do not automatically infer intelligence when regularity could result from inherent tendencies of will-as-thing-in-itself or blind physical laws—compare explanatory merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: External design differs when end and means lie in different individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: This already occurs in organised nature, in a certain degree, when the design is an external one, i.e., the end lies in one individual and the means in another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize cases of 'external' teleology (e.g., ecological interactions, coadaptations) where the functional end of one organism is realized through another; interpret such designs as part of teleological accounting but note the separation of end and means across individuals complicates causal attribution.
